Arthur Feiner Ph.D.

Arthur Feiner

Arthur Feiner  

THE EDITORS MOURN THE PASSING of Helen Ekstein, who had served this Journal (among her many responsibilities at the William Alanson White Institute) since its inception. This she accomplished diligently, with that special, smiling grace for which she was well known. She handled all the Journal's editorial correspondence, kept the records of manuscripts received, and organized the cover, contents, index and books-received pages. This issue was the last on which she worked. Since she was the Journal's direct link to authors, mailing acceptance and rejection notices, in a sense she was the Journal's public representative. And she acquitted this task pleasantly, eagerly and expertly. She was the Journal's most avid fan and supporter with constant energetic efforts on its behalf, especially in the warm, friendly way she carried out her endless tasks. No longer will the answering machine announce sweetly, "It's Helen … there's a nice letter from that man in South Dakota. Call when you have time." And no longer will we think, "I'll call Helen Monday morning to find out what happened to that manuscript." With her direct, altruistic, vivacious, yet gentle style, she secured a permanent place in our hearts.

Metaphor and Reality—A Response to Roy Schafer

Russell Meares M.D.

Russell Meares

Russell Meares, M.D.
Department of Psychiatry University of Sydney Westmead Centre
Westmead, N.S.W. 2145
Australia

Russell Meares  

All life reveals itself as a continuous interchange between an inner and an outer world.
Karl Jaspers, p. 12.

THIS PAPER CONSIDERS THE IMPORT of Jaspers' view—contemplates, indeed, the possibility that it has no use at all. This consideration is prompted by the growing acceptance of the thesis that the concept of an inner world is logically impossible and therapeutically harmful (Schafer, 1976), (1983). We are necessarily led to fundamental issues—of how, for example, we sense our existence and of how this elusive apprehension might be expressed. The argument clearly has a philosophical flavour not generally associated with psychiatric dissertations. Nevertheless, since Schafer states that he has derived his approach from such sources, it demands examination, however brief.

What follows is an unusual dialectic. Thesis and antithesis evolve toward no synthesis; rather, the conclusion shows their irreconcilable, revealing two quite different traditions of thought within the psychoanalytic movement. Schafer himself is a distinguished representative of one of these traditions; Winnicott gave original expression to the views of an alternative.

In brief, the argument revolves around the value of the spatial metaphor of self, which Schafer rejects but which others find useful both theoretically and therapeutically (e.g., Davis and Wallbridge, 1983).

Schafer has performed the valuable service of pointing out that the language of metapsychology is based on metaphor and should be recognized as such.

SILVERMAN AND LACHMANN have presented some of the research findings in support of their hypothesis that the arousal of unconscious oneness fantasies may encourage adaptive responses. They further argue that their data is consistent with Kohut's (1977) therapeutic use of empathic responsiveness with developmentally arrested patients.

Silverman's (1967), (1969), (1975) research indicates that stimuli that are out of conscious awareness can motivate us in either helpful or disruptive ways. This repeated finding offers an experimental demonstration of the functioning of the unconscious. His, by now classic, experiments indicate that when aggressive stimuli are subliminally presented to schizophrenic patients there is an increase in disordered thinking. Stimuli geared to the particular psychodynamic constellations of other diagnostic groups, increased their symptomotology as well. These findings corroborate the psychoanalytic theory of psychopathology. When derivatives of unconscious conflictual wishes press for expression, symptoms emerge.

If particular subliminal stimuli trigger psychopathology, the researchers reasoned, other stimuli should reduce pathology. They have found that the "Mommy and I Are One" stimulus does, in fact, diminish symptomatology in a number of subject populations.

Murray Krim Ph.D.

Murray Krim

Murray Krim  

Ralph Manning Crowley was part of the history of the psychoanalytic movement in the United States. He shared its youth and early, spirited growth. He was deeply involved in its refreshing newness and excitement, and was passionate about the ideas of the intellectual innovative giants who were his teachers, colleagues, and later, friends.

Ralph was born in Madison, Wisconsin, in 1905. His father was an executive of a retail lumber business, his mother a housewife and, after her husband's death, a social worker and remedial reading teacher. He attended public and private schools in Madison, and later, the Phillips Academy in Massachusetts. At the University of Wisconsin in 1924, he studied under Norman Cameron. He was graduated from the University with honors, and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa. He completed a M.A. in psychology in 1928, and soon enrolled in the Northwestern University Medical School to prepare for the study of psychiatry. Here he met Lionel Blitzsten, just returned from Europe and enthusiastic about his analysis with Franz Alexander. Encouraged and stimulated by this new wave of exciting psychoanalytic thinking, Ralph became an analysand of Blitzsten. In 1932 he began psychoanalytic training at the newly formed Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute, where Alexander, French, Horney and Blitzsten were faculty members. It was a most impassioned time. Nazism was darkening the horizon in Europe and the arrival of emigré analysts began to infuse American progressive psychiatric thinking with new provocative and energizing ideas.

In 1934, Ralph began a residency at Sheppard and Enoch Pratt Hospital in Baltimore. Many of the staff became involved in the Washington School of Psychiatry (founded 1936). These included Lewis B. Arthur Feiner  

WE AT THE EDITORSHIP OF this Journal, had an abiding respect and affection for Ralph M. Crowley, his being our sometime admissions interviewer, sometime critic, sometime guide and advisor, sometime teacher and supervisor, sometime conservationist and sometime raconteur. His death last year was a loss to all. He was always encouraging, and especially helpful to us, when asked, treading inevitably with light foot. He was our link to a noble, adventuresome and intellectual past, the American frontier spirit of discovery and pluralism, the ferment of the Mid-West during the early part of this century, and the ebullient rise and spread of enlightenment within our profession. As would be expected of such a man, when he served as editorial reader, his reviews of manuscripts usually found someting good in each despite an otherwise perceptive, trenchant, critical evaluation. He was of firm, humanistic bent, confidently rooted in, and attentive to the standards of classicism. His presence on the Publication Committee of the William Alanson White Institute added his own touch of dignity, wit and wisdom. This issue is dedicated to him and all that he represented to us.

THE READER OF THE PROCESS OF PSYCHOANALYTIC THERAPY cannot help but admire and respect its author, Emanuel Peterfreund. The book is, in many senses, a landmark volume. In striking contrast to the dearth of writings on the subject of psychoanalytic validation, Peterfreund boldly and in remarkably straight-forward fashion offers the most comprehensive clinical and theoretical discussion of the topic available in the literature. Rightfully mindful of the near total neglect of issues of confirmation evident in clinical psychoanalytic work, as well as in the pertinent literature, Peterfreund boldly demonstrates the existence of a common failing in this regard and, more importantly, proposes definitive remedies. He is uniquely candid in his critique of the clinical writings of other psychoanalysts, and he offers convincing evidence of the rampant use among clinicians of preformed theoretical constructs, of restricted and prejudiced formulations, of concepts and interpretations that clearly lack support in the material from patients, and of basically meaningless psychoanalytic clichés and intellectualizations. The need for clinical reform is rendered more than evident, and Peterfreund carefully outlines the heuristic approach to classical psychoanalysis as a sound corrective. Furthermore, by presenting specific clinical excerpts, Peterfreund explicitly defines the strategies of psychoanalysis which he is advocating and provides the reader ample opportunity to examine and test out his hypotheses, formulations, and interpretations through his or her own independent assessment. In all, this is a truly unique psychoanalytic effort at clinical definition and precision.

MEARES'S REVIEW OF MY WORK on action language is based on misreading. A brief response should suffice to indicate the problems.

Meares's review rests in large part on allegations concerning my positions on metaphor, reality, and the conduct of therapy. He presents me as so devoted to logic over phenomenology as to be consistently negative in my attitude toward metaphor. According to comments he makes in different places, I reject metaphor altogether, I find the metaphor of the inner world therapeutically harmful, I disparage metaphor because there is no "it" that metaphor refers to, metaphor is not real, and it cannot be validated.

What is the actual case? I developed a critique of metapsychology as the theoretical language for psychoanalysis. (Here, by the way, and contrary to Meares's wrong account of it, is where I drew on Binswanger, Sartre, and Wittgenstein). Going further, I proposed an alternative language in which to couch the theoretical propositions of psychoanalysis, and I named it action language. I emphasized how often Freud and others fell back on blatant metaphor to get over the logical rough spots of metapsychology.

DOES OUR PROFESSION APPEAR "impossible" and which we nevertheless hopefully pursue, and the task "impossible", at least one that has no closure? Perhaps that's the truth underlying the feeling of "impossible"—that we have no closure.

Truth! Are we seeking the one grand monolithic truth? Or, as a contemporary philosopher, John Herman Randall, once said, "There is not the truth, but there are many truths." Perhaps it is the case that truth and truths come in all sizes, that some are grand and monolithic and have the quality of "things", of nouns, and some deal with processes, capturing the spirit of verbs. Some are statements of meaning, offered with assured certainty, as the meaning of the universe.

Is personal truth to be revealed through the psychoanalytic enterprise, or rather the truths concerning the inner processes, the outer impingements that shape our lives, our choices that shape our lives?

Anna Antonovsky  

I

PSYCHOANALYSIS AS A METHOD OF CURE assumes a need for or a tendency toward integration. This tendency has been described as or attributed to the pressure of the unconscious or repressed to become conscious, the working of Eros seeking to unite units and objects, and/or to the integrative capacities of the ego. These are obviously abstractions utilized to express the idea that the human being seems to have the need, as we might put it in the idiom of our day, to "get it together"—to get aspects of the self together, to establish links between different psychic experiences, to make connections with others. Getting things together does not exclude differentiation and taking cognizance of reality; on the contrary, it is furthered by them. But certain inescapable discrepancies in maturation and development, likely traumata and perhaps even constitutional imbalances are seen as throwing up powerful obstacles which become part of the psyche and act to disrupt and hinder the integrative trends. Internal conflict or discontinuity is therefore inevitable. The persistance of conflict is abetted by resistance, by the reluctance or unwillingness to become aware of conflict and to engage one's energies toward its resolution. The analytic attempt to cure is the attempt to facilitate integration by way of working with the resistances. Mutative work in psychoanalysis is the successful overcoming of resistance.

The notion of inherently integrative forces at work can be referred to a biological or an organismic model, without thereby reducing psychoanalysis to biology. Both the patient's experience which we deal with and the process we engage ourselves in with the other person seem to me to have an organic-like quality. Psychoanalysis does not follow a linear sequence. It has, rather, a Gestalt character, reaching for closure.

Insofar as the integration is with another, it takes on the form of a dialogue under pressure.

IT IS AN OFTEN ATTESTED discovery in the supervision of candidates in psychoanalytic training that the excellence of their work rests only slightly on their thoretical knowledge. Sometimes their work appears much better where their theoretical knowledge is least, and at all events particular theoretical predilections rather rarely affect their competence or even their style as analysts. There are extremes, of course; and I cannot go so far as to say that it makes no difference at all what their theory is. I have after all supervised candidates of only one psychoanalytic institute, and that one fairly traditionally devoted to the ego psychology that achieved orthodox status in the 1940's, although our faculty have not been insensible to other developments. It is further always moot to what extent theory once learned subtly influences technique even after its fetters have been rationally shrugged off. Many of us whose psychoanalytic education took place in the '40's and '50's were firmly indoctrinated by injunctions to strict defense analysis that even decades of corrective experience have not fully erased.

For all that, analyst and supervisor, in the absence of excessive strains or tensions in the character of either, may sit comfortably together confronting the analyst's reports of his sessions with the patient without too much regard to the higher flights of theory. Following some remarks by Lacan (1977, pp. 44–45), I may point here to what actually occurs in supervision. The task of the supervisor is to recognize in the dialogue reported by the candidate, unconscious elements in the discourse of the patient that the candidate has not himself or herself recognized. Better still when possible the supervisor may corroborate independently the candidate's inferences, in which case the sense of conviction of both parties is the stronger. Best of all, perhaps, are those gratifying occasions when the supervisor can be shown by the analyst in training to be wrong in his inferences.

Human reactions of analysts to patients Samiksa, 6:212–219, 1952

I BELIEVE THAT THE HUMAN EMOTIONAL REACTIONS of analysts to their patients not only cannot be avoided, but can be used to facilitate analytic understanding and progress.

Similarly, an analyst may have rational and reality based feelings and attitudes toward his patient, which I do not include in my use of the term counter-transference. Some authors use that term to include these appropriate, unexaggerated non-defensive, and non-anxious reactions of an analyst to patients. These responses, however, are neither counter, that is, provoked only by the patient, nor are they transference reactions in the sense of being unanalyzed and irrational. They are much neglected. Their significance is belittled and their usefulness to therapy is not realized.

… from noticing at any given moment our own reactions with patients, we, as analysts, can learn much about what our patients are really like and what they are doing with us in the analysis.

The following pieces, by Ralph Crowley, were excerpted from some of his writings. His dedication to the clarification of Harry Stack Sullivan's ideas is evident, as was Crowley's timely, clinical acumen and originality.

PSYCHOPATHOLOGY MAY BE VIEWED as the result of the interference of an alien culture with the unfolding of biologically given behavioral sequences (1982). There is an affinity between this ethological point of view, as set forth by Bowlby, and the ideas of one of the founders of the interpersonal-cultural school, i.e., Erich Fromm.

I shall base myself mainly on Man for Himself, which I consider Fromm's most seminal work. I shall present the ethological viewpoint, offering it as a critique of Western European bourgeois society, much like Fromm's. After a review of Bowlby's attachment theory, I shall suggest extensions and integrate these with ethological aspects of Fromm's work.

The Ethological Viewpoint

The ethological viewpoint could be summarized as follows. The human species is characterized by a prevalence of culture influence in interaction with biological potential. The opposite holds true at the beginning of development. The biologically determined behavior we observe in the infant, and the complementary response it evokes in caretaking adults, emerged in the course of evolution because of their survival value. The environment to which our innate behavior is adapted is called by Bowlby the "environment of evolutionary adaptedness."

In the history of man, cultural evolution has modified the environment at an increasing pace. Culture itself has become a manmade environment to which man has had to adapt—a filter between himself and nature (Rosenthal, 1971). The rate of cultural evolution has far outstripped that of man's biological evolution.

I WASN'T ABLE TO DECIDE what this panel was supposed to be about. It seemed to me that psychoanalytic training had to provide an education, during which the trainee had better have an experience. I thought over my own training and decided I had indeed been educated and I could talk about that. And what an experience! One of my supervisors wore black shirts and ties and smoked cigarettes in a very long, thin cigarette holder in an absent-minded way. I was afriad he would burn himself. I used to watch the ashes drop onto the carpet and wondered what the message was. I didn't like black shirts. I wondered if I would have to learn to like black shirts. And everyone, candidates and faculty, were either getting married or divorced, or remarried. The only stable faculty members seemed to be the bachelors and spinsters.

Erich Fromm told us, in all humility, that there was little to teach since little was known and, indeed that some people seemed to him to have therapeutic personalities and that others seemed untrainable.

Anita Tenzer Ph.D.

Anita Tenzer

Anita Tenzer, Ph.D.
45 East 89th Street

Anita Tenzer  

THERE IS A REVOLUTION going on in psychoanalysis. Ultimate truths may be giving way to functional realities, arbitrary laws to relative truths. "New truths" or facets of knowledge are emerging that cut across metapsychological boundaries. I hope to show that from the point of view of Piaget's genetic epistemology, the same processes are operative in the construction of new truths in psychoanalytic theory as in the construction of new truths within the psychoanalytic dyad.

One of the problems with psychoanalytic theorizing is that models of the mind and clinical observations have become so interwoven that sometimes neither is clear. If we pay attention to personality organization and development on the one hand and therapeutic processes on the other, rather than both at once, we may be able to partial out what is "true" across the smörgesbord of psychoanalytic theory. A major move in this direction was spear-headed by George Klein (1973) who separated "metapsychological theory" from "clinical theory, " the latter having to do with psychoanalytic processes. I shall be addressing clinical theory, not metapsychology.

In this paper, I am concerned with the construction of new truths in clinical theory and with the parallel construction of new truths by analyst and analysand in the psychoanalytic situation, as seen from the perspective of Piaget's work on the development of knowledge.

For Piaget, knowledge is constantly being re-invented or restructured by the individual's active participation in his world, especially by his interaction with other people. Cognition is motivated by affect. Knowledge is a continuous construction that is activated in response to a need. In science, nothing is discovered unless there is curiosity and an active quest for knowledge. The same holds true in analysis. The scientist—like the analyst—is a participant observer and is constantly affecting the world he is discovering. In the same way, the interaction between analyst and patient affects and shapes their respective ways of seeing and being in the world.

RAGE IS A COMMON CLINICAL PROBLEM for which there has been little agreement on an effective therapeutic approach. Perhaps no issues in psychotherapy have divided different schools and different therapists so deeply and so consistently as have their approaches to anger and aggression in psychotherapy and their clinical prescriptions for the treatment of rage. Some therapists see the experience of rage as inherently harmful to the growth of the patient and to the goals of psychotherapy and would treat it as a problem to be met at all times with vigorous confrontation and vigilant limit-setting. Others describe the expression of rage in psychotherapy as intrinsically curative and a therapeutic goal in itself, the "primal scream" therapy of Janov (1970) being the extreme example. Even among psychoanalytic writers there have been profound differences of approach to the treatment of rage. Although many of these differences are rooted in fundamentally divergent concepts of psychopathology and may be irreconcilable, the function and sources of rage in personal development, its meaning in the therapeutic context, and the problems of a therapeutic response to rage have seldom been jointly and systematically considered. To clarify our therapeutic options the integration of developmental and clinical perspectives is essential. In this paper I will address this task in a preliminary way.

A DETACHED HISTORIAN WILL SOME DAY be able to describe a natural history of the response of psychoanalysts to innovations. This may be similar to the response to the innovations that occur in other disciplines as well, but such group responses among psychoanalysts are intensified, perhaps, due to covert, unacknowledged identifications and counter-identifications with the attitudes held by one's training analyst—a much more complex relationship than exists between a student and a teacher. There is, initially, a period of polarization which may continue for generations. Gradually however, ideas that are clinically valid become unobtrusively incorporated into what is a generally accepted view, and the heretical source is conveniently forgotten. Something of this sort has happened with some of Melanie Klein's proposals. If one leaves her improbable time table of early psychic development aside, many of her observations have been quietly incorporated into the main stream of psychoanalytic thought: the importance of early ambivalence, the process of splitting and the significance of introjective and projective processes, and most important, the fact that a certain quantum of guilt will evoke the need to make restitution. Some authors who were in the main stream of psychoanalysis, such as Edith Jacobson (1964), did openly identify Melanie Klein as the source of some valued clinical observations, but others who also relied heavily on her work found it more politic to remain silent.

THERE ARE CERTAIN WISHES and fantasies, typically unconscious, that are directed toward a state of oneness with another person; in the terminology of psychoanalysis, a state in which, to varying degrees, representations of self and object are merged. In The Search For Oneness(Silverman, Lachmann and Milich, 1982), we considered the presence of these wishes and fantasies in a variety of human activities. We cited numerous references in the psychoanalytic literature to what clinicians commonly refer to as symbiotic wishes—unconscious wishes of adult patients with various forms of psychopathology for a kind of union with a gratifying maternal figure. We argued that these unconscious wishes of union with the "good mother" of infancy underlie the frequently appearing expressions in adults of unconscious oneness fantasies; i.e., fantasies of having obtained a state of oneness with important figures in the individual's life. However, we left open the possibility that these oneness fantasies may, at times, be rooted in later phases of development, including the oedipal period and may involve father, as well as mother, as the sought for object of merger.

THE HISTORY OF TRAINING ANALYSIS is almost as old as psychoanalysis itself. Early, Freud stated that the analyzing instrument, the analyst, must understand the process from the inside; that is, he must undergo an analysis himself as a cornerstone of his training.

At one time, the training analysis and the supervision of a candidate were done by the same analyst. The basic assumption was that the personal analysis and supervision, along with course work, were all parts of the student's education. Hence, the term "training analysis" or "didactic analysis."

This made for considerable anxiety for both analysand and analyst. It introduced extra-analytic issues stemming from the candidate's need to graduate, and to advance within the structure of the analytic institute. Thus, the candidate's need to please by being the good patient may be operative.

EMPATHY ON THE PART OF A THERAPIST for his patient is universally regarded as indispensable for useful psychoanalytic therapy to occur. Although there are differences in definitions of empathy, the capacity to empathize receives a very high priority in the selection process of therapist training programs across disciplines, thus attesting to its significance. The absence of empathy is often mentioned in assessments of stormy countertransference developments. This paper examines disruptions in the empathic process, with special emphasis upon the phenomenon of projective identification. In so doing, we build upon a previous contribution (Tansey and Burke, 1985) which elucidated the relationship between empathy in the therapist and projective identification from the patient. In attempting to clarify the varieties of empathic disruption, we shall address the question of whether empathy is teachable in the training of psychoanalytic therapists.

As a consequence of variability within the literature, our definitions of empathy and projective identification must be specified. We will then review the conclusions of our earlier companion paper, as well as the relevant literature on empathic disruptions, before coming to the main body of our current thesis. We view empathy as a clinical phenomenon characterized by two primary components which unfold with varying degrees of awareness either gradually over many sessions or, more commonly, in what seems like an immediate "flash." The initial component involves what Fliess (1942) refers to as the therapist's "trial identification" with his patient.

DONALD WINNICOTT DEVELOPED HIS CONTRIBUTION to the psychoanalytic dialogue in the intellectual and social climate of the British Psychoanalytical Society of the 1920's through early 70's. The British Society during much of this period was sharply and often bitterly divided between the ideas and personalities of Anna Freud and Melanie Klein. Winnicott was analyzed first by James Strachey and then by Joan Rivière, one of the early Kleinian "inner circle;" he was supervised by Melanie Klein in his psychoanalytic work with children. Although Winnicott's thinking developed in a direction different from that of Klein, he never denounced Kleinian thinking as did many analysts who had been at one point open to Klein's ideas (e.g. Glover [1945] and Schmideberg [1935]).

Winnicott was a dialectician. His thinking thrived in the medium of the intense debate between the classical Freudian and the Kleinian groups. He understood that once we feel that we have finally resolved a basic psychoanalytic issue (either in our theory or in our understanding of patients), it is at that point that our thinking has reached an impasse. THIS PAPER FOCUSES ON THE RELATIONSHIP between mother and daughter and its effect on the daughter's reaction to success. Mothers play a special, sometimes crucial, role in the psychology of women as the original source of nourishment, sensual gratification, and gender identification. If the mother does not encourage and reinforce her daughter for fear that she herself may be surpassed and feel superfluous, the resulting discouragement can undermine the daughter and result in extreme anxiety and a tendency to fail. The fear of failure is usually conscious. The fear of success is apt to be unconscious (Tec, 1976). A daughter can become fearful of the competition of other women, afraid of their disapproval, and, as a consequence, sabotage her own development. Success is seen as a demand, not as a legitimate result of skill and competence. In the recent past much emphasis has been placed on the positive role of the father in encouraging the growth of his daughter, but a father's encouragement can also result in inhibitions related to Oedipal guilt (Moulton, 1977). The daughter may come to feel "unentitled" to her victories, particularly when she sees that she has "surpassed" the mother. Since the role of men in "keeping women down" has been the subject of so much publicity in recent years, I have chosen to focus on the mother's influence. My emphasis is on fear of disapproval, rage, and competition from other women, not just the familiar prejudice and societal focus on male discrimination.

PSYCHOANALYSIS, IN ADDITION TO WHATEVER else it may be, is a process of knowing and understanding oneself. This self-knowledge is the means to help us become free from the psychic constrictions that impede our living. What is the nature of this self-knowledge

though, and when it is ("truth") achieved? I would like to propose a schema which suggests that psychoanalysis has undergone several periods, each of which is marked by a central theme concerning how psychoanalytic knowledge and truth are to be understood. I will describe the manner in which these periods are reflective of larger philosophical developments in the history of ideas and of views of truth in general.

My focus here is on the practice or doing of psychoanalysis as a process of knowing—less so on a "body of knowledge" or a "theory of man". I offer the schema not for the purposes of classification per se, rather as an expository device to describe some significant epistemological trends in the field. My characterization therefore is with a rather broad brush stroke without explicating in detail the particular elements of larger themes.

Overview of Schema

A brief overview of what I'll more fully describe is that Freud launched psychoanalysis under the umbrella of a pervasive view of knowledge and truth in which truth is reified. According to this view, knowledge and truth are found by locating the correct representation in the mind to correspond to an essence out there. One of the legacies of this has been the importance of metapsychology within psychoanalysis. Developments in several directions of 20th century thinking have converged toward a fundamental critique of this view of knowledge. As these critical ideas have impacted on psychoanalysis, there has been a general epistemological trend away from the preeminence of metapsychology, to a refocusing on the features of the actual communicative encounter between analyst and patient. Another way of saying this, is that the clinical situation itself becomes the key attraction to anyone interested in understanding the nature, limits and conditions of psychoanalytic knowing and knowledge.

BEGINNING IN THE LATE 1940S AND EARLY 1950S countertransference began to be viewed from a new perspective. It became established, in some circles, that countertransference, originally considered a hindrance to the analytic work, constituted a source of analytic data not always obtainable from the patient's associations. (See Epstein and Feiner, 1979, for a summary of the literature).

With our increasing appreciation of the interpersonal nature of the analytic situation and the dialectic of the transference-countertransference interaction (see Ehrenberg, 1982), (1984, for a summary of the literature) it has become commonplace also to think of countertransference as an integral aspect of the analytic relationship, and to recognize that it has its impact on the patient whether or not we are aware of it. Because countertransference can be either a threat to analytic efforts or facilitate them, what has become clear is that it is incumbent on us to learn how to use it with sensitivity so that a genuine analytic process is maintained. One irony facing us, therefore, is that the growth of the movement in this direction has helped underscore the real dangers of misuse, and this in turn has served, to some extent, to reinforce traditional concerns about the risks involved, as well as natural tendencies to countertransference resistance.

The analyst's resistance to his awareness that there are countertransference problems, including resistance to the awareness of such resistance, precludes the possibility of utilizing countertransference data in the analysis. It actually increases the likelihood of countertransference affecting the work in less than optimal ways, thereby confirming the traditional hindrance point of view (Freud, 1910).

The "Bogged Down" Treatment: A Remedy

Allan Cooper Ph.D. and Earl Witenberg M.D.

Earl Witenberg

Allan Cooper, Ph.D.
Earl G. Witenberg, M.D.
20 West 74th Street
New York, New York 10023

Earl Witenberg  

MOST ANALYSTS ARE FAMILIAR with what happens when a treatment situation gets bogged down. The same issues are discussed over and over, unrelated issues are raised, and both patient and analyst become repetitively monotonous. An atmosphere of boredom pervades the situation; a feeling of not being understood. The sense of dissatisfaction which characterizes the bogged-down treatment ranges from a vague unease to a marked feeling of despair.

The customary reasons given for this unproductive experience may be characterized as either hopeless or hopeful. Hopeless reasons are the patient is (1) diagnostically unsuitable; or (2) is too regressed. Seemingly hopeful reasons are (1) unconscious, abstruse dynamics will emerge eventually or, (2) transference-countertransference issues have not been sufficiently clarified and need to be explored.

It is our contention that these "reasons" are usually invoked because of stereotyped preconceptions. Therefore, the analysis will become unproductive. Stating the "hopeless" reasons leads to either stopping treatment or making treatment non-analytic. On the other hand, waiting for dynamics to emerge will perpetuate the original dilemma. "Optimistically, " pursuing transference-countertransference issues, with the hope of discovering some new subtle issue, will lead to increased entanglement without enhancing clarity.

All or any of the above reasons may certainly be true; however we have found that a much more frequent cause of bogged-down treatment lies in the failure of the analyst to elicit a coherent overview of the patient in the beginning of treatment.

IT IS WELL THAT THE INVITATION to participate in this panel came along when it did; that is before I forgot my own descent or ascent into this profession. When we are young we don't know how ignorant we are, and when we are old we forget. But I have never forgotten my first interview. That interview and its subsequent developments still seem fantastic and incredible to me today.

In the 35 years that have elapsed since I became an analyst I have never come across a patient or candidate in analysis who was as naive as I was at the time when I started. I wish I had. My personal analysis exerted an enormous influence on my life. It was an adventure in self-discovery: a painful and very exacting undertaking, perhaps among the hardest things I have gone through in my life. Because of the impact the analytic experience had on me, I have said many times, and still say: that if you've had this experience you will never forget it, and if you have never had it you will never believe it.

I don't think that it is a good idea to use this occasion for a biographical account of our struggle to become psychoanalysts. But I think that much will be gained if we allow ourselves to be somewhat personal in sharing our views, since we've all had experience both as trainees and as teachers. It might lead to a more fruitful discussion, as we continue to learn from our experience.

Michael Friedman M.D.

Michael Friedman

Michael Friedman, M.D.
921 The Alameda

Michael Friedman  

FREUD'S CONCEPTUALIZATION OF GUILT, stated most clearly in Civilization and Its Discontents, remains the predominant conceptualization of guilt in psychoanalysis although it is embedded in a theory of motivation (drive theory) that has been increasingly rejected. According to Freud, guilt is the fear of an internalized threat of loss of love and loss of protection from a variety of dangers. While it is difficult to overestimate the importance of the fear of an internalized threat of loss of love as a motivation in human life, I do not believe that this concept represents what people ordinarily mean by guilt. More importantly, it has, in my opinion, obscured a significant line of human motivation and has impeded the effective treatment of a wide range of psychopathology. The purposes of this paper are (1) to examine Freud's concept of guilt; (2) to review some recent research and theory in developmental psychology and evolutionary biology which point to an alternative concept of guilt; (3) to review several attempts within psychoanalysis to modify or supplement Freud's concept of guilt, all of which can be seen as efforts to move toward this alternative concept; (4) to make some tentative suggestions toward a reconceptualization of guilt; and (5) to illustrate some clinical implications of this reconceptualization.

This paper has grown out of my participation in the Mount Zion Psychotherapy Research Project led by Joseph Weiss and Harold Sampson, whose insight into the importance of unconscious guilt in psychopathology has inspired the research of our group as well as this essay (Weiss, Sampson, et al, 1986). THE IMPETUS FOR SELECTION OF THE THEME, "Psychoanalysis and Truth: Current Issues, " was the excitement and controversy currently being aroused by the introduction into psychoanalysis of constructivist ideas about the nature of knowledge (Barratt, 1984) ; (Loch, 1977) ; (Ricoeur, 1977) ; (Schafer, 1983) ; (Spence, 1982) ; (Steele, 1979) ; (Viderman, 1979). As it is used here, constructivism is a label for a broad movement in the contemporary thought of many fields, a movement based on

… the growing awareness that any so-called reality is—in the most immediate and concrete sense—the construction of those who believe they have discovered and investigated it. In other words, what is found is an invention whose inventor is unaware of his act of invention, who considers it as something that exists independently of him … (Watzlawick, 1984, p. 10).

Robert Langs  

WHILE SERIOUS CONSIDERATION OF THE unconscious communication between patient and analyst had its origins at the turn of the century (Freud, 1900), there are many who believe that its full elaboration still lies ahead of us. It seems likely now that it will require a full century of struggle before psychoanalysts have borne the ripest fruits of this level of understanding. Derived from Freud's (1900) model of the relationship between the day residue and the dream—basically a stimulus and response paradigm—the ramifications of investigations of the spiraling conscious and, especially, unconscious communicative interaction between patient and therapist or analyst (the two will be used interchangeably in this paper) are surprisingly extensive. This presentation will describe the basic components of the communicative approach, detail critical aspects of its most recent thinking as a means of bridging the present and the future, and will conclude by indicating fresh problems that have been crystalized through these endeavors and whose solutions lie ahead of us.

It seems likely that the communicative approach will be one of several avenues that will restore psychoanalysis to its rightful leadership in the study of human psychopathology (madness) and its cure. Much of the loss of faith in both psychoanalytic theory and technique, including their application to psychoanalytic psychotherapy, has arisen because of the failure of psychoanalysts to recognize the flaws in their theory and clinical endeavors.

ATTENTION TO ADULT DEVELOPMENT is a relatively recent phenomenon in psychoanalysis and attempts to incorporate clinical knowledge of adult development into an overall development schema have been fragmentary.

Development is a concept that implies continuity and growth; adult development theory, to the extent that it exists in the analytic field has tended to be discontinuous, vague, romanticized, focussed solely on loss or limited to the socio-cultural at the expense of intrapsychic considerations. Writers seem to have a more consistent notion of adult development across the life-span than psychoanalysts. Goethe's (1944)Faust, Thomas Mann's (1913)Death in Venice or the contemporary " The Color Purple " by Alice Walker (1983) would not have been written without a view of development as lifelong. Analysts tend to support the notion that psychological growth occurs throughout life; and yet one cannot help but feel that the prevailing professional opinion sees psychoanalysis as a prerequisite for mature adulthood. Horney is a minority of one when she writes "fortunately psychoanalysis is not the only way to resolve inner conflicts. Life itself still remains a very effective therapist" (Horney, 1945, p. 240).

Michael Tansey Ph.D. and Walter Burke Ph.D.

Walter Burke  

PSYCHOANALYTIC THERAPY IS A PROCESS fully involving two individuals who exert a mutual and ongoing influence upon one another. In what follows, we shall examine the manner in which a patient may allow himself to be understood by the therapist through the communicative properties of interpersonal influence in the therapeutic interaction. We hope to clarify the ways in which "interactional communications" from the patient may be understood and utilized by the therapist. The term interactional communication refers to all communications, both in words and in actions, which are transmitted through the interaction consciously and unconsciously by both patient and therapist.

In so doing, we propose to demonstrate that in the process of a therapist achieving empathic contact, the mechanism of projective identification from the patient is always involved; and conversely, that when a patient engages in projective identification, there is always the potential for the therapist to achieve an empathic outcome, whether or not this potential is actualized. Although previously thought to be unrelated—if not downright antipathetic—we intend to establish that empathy and projective identification represent interrelated aspects of a unitary sequence for the therapist's processing of interactional communications.

Although we emphasize our view of psychoanalytic therapy as a radically mutual process, we shall concern ourselves primarily with an examination of the experience of the therapist-in-interaction.

Roberta Held-Weiss  

ONE EVENING RECENTLY, a prominent speaker, a man who has written many books and who comes from a venerable tradition, presented a clinical discussion before a distinguished audience of analysts. In it he outlined in great and touching detail the data: the early infantile deprivations and subsequent losses sustained by a man who throughout his long and very productive life suffered great anguish of spirit and unsatisfying object relations. He offered clinical formulations which had not only coherence and power but which also, he thought, accounted for the patient's regressive yearning and search for the absent mother typical of pathological mourning. Early and repeated deprivation, it was said, determined his adult character, and the effort at reparation led, at the deepest level, to the subject's creativity. In corroboration images were deciphered and similar findings among a significant number of patients with early parent loss were offered to substantiate the theoretical claims and confirm diagnostic predictions. An appreciative discussion closed the meeting. At the end of the presentation, many people in the audience applauded, a significant number of psychoanalysts however, felt their own thought and experience had not been represented. I was one of them. I thought to myself, "This is not the state of the art in psychoanalysis. Prescriptive encoding and causal historical explanation do not account for the vitality of contemporary psychoanalytic thought. The heart of the psychoanalytic endeavor is not in this kind of closed form and exclusiveness of construction." Though we long for order, predetermined truth speaks to an order which the experience of psychoanalysis itself belies.

It will be my thesis that the truth we look for in psychoanalysis is not to be found while searching for historical events or causes, nor in recreating, restoring, or repairing the past. Neither would I locate it in a hermeneutic exegesis, a coherent and logical narrative. Instead I would search for it in our patients' struggle to give shape and meaning to their experience, in their efforts, however fragmented, unordered, incoherent, desultory, erratic or formless these efforts may be.

OVER THE PAST FORTY YEARS, psychoanalysts have paid increasing attention to either end of the span of childhood years. At one end of this span the recent studies of infancy have altered our appreciation for the complexities of the neonate. The newborn, it has turned out, is far better organized than was postulated by psychoanalytic theory.

At the other end of the span of childhood years, Freud's (1916 [1915]) study of transience and Kohut's (1966) elaboration of the forms and transformations of narcissism have addressed some of the tasks of the adult years. The range of years during which psychological organization, reorganization, formation and transformation, takes place have been stretched from birth to death.

With respect to the adult years, Erikson's (1950) pioneering work still offers a perspective to which current investigators turn. His epigenetic model has been reevaluated in the light of longitudinal and cross-sectional studies by Gould (1978), Vailliant (1977) and others. Fitzpatrick and Friedman (1983) in their survey of this literature conclude:

The psychological issues a person wrestles with in all stages of his life invariably recur as he wrestles with new issues at later stages. Development may not be portrayed merely or primarily as a linear progression but needs to be viewed as a spiral or tapestry in which multiple interactions simultaneously link the past and the present. As a person labors with each stage, he simultaneously repeats, albeit in different terms, the issues of all prior stages. Therefore, adult development is at once similar to, different from, and an extension of childhood development (p. 411).

THE SUPERVISORY PROCESS HAS RECEIVED considerable attention in the psychoanalytic literature recently (Bromberg, 1982) ; (Caligor, 1981) ; (Cooper and Witenberg, 1983) ; (Gediman and Wolkenfeld, 1980) ; (Issacharoff, 1982) ; (Lederman, 1982) ; (Lesser, 1983) ; (Levenson, 1982) ; (Wolstein, 1984). Several writers (Bromberg, 1982) ; (Caligor, 1981) ; (Gediman and Wolkenfeld, 1980) ; (Lederman, 1982) have focused on the parallel process phenomenon. Bromberg's (1982) and Caligor's (1981) studies of parallel and reciprocal processes examine, from an interpersonal and operational perspective, how transference and countertransference in the analytic relationship provoke parataxes in the supervisory dyad. 1The term parataxis is used here in the sense of parataxic distortion(Sullivan, 1940) ; i.e., as referring to the transferential dimension of human living. In Sullivan's words (p. 92), an "… integration is parataxic, … when, besides the interpersonal situation as defined within the awareness of the speaker, there is a concomitant interpersonal situation quite different as to its principal integrating tendencies, of which the speaker is more or less completely unaware.

Besides the two-group integrated of psychiatrist [i.e., object] and subject there is in the parataxic situation, also an illusory two-group integrated of psychiatrist [i.e., object]—distorted-to-accommodate-a-special-'you'-pattern and subject-reliving-an-earlier-unresolved-integration-and-manifesting-the corresponding-special-'me'-pattern."

Sullivan (1953) referred more broadly to parataxis as one of three modes of human experience, developmentally intermediate between prototaxic and syntaxic experience. Parataxis, in this wider sense, includes non-rational (prelogical) intuitive processes, along with irrational and distorted experience. There may be instances in this paper when both senses of the term fit. The reader is referred to Mullahy (1970), Schecter (1971), and Grey (1982) for further discussion of this concept.

I WISH TO EXPRESS MY PLEASURE at being here at a neighbor institute. I am honored to participate in your fortieth anniversary. Yours is an institute with a great tradition in New York City.

At another institute, with which I am most familiar, and I suspect in most institutes, there is a common observation of beginning analytic candidates with their first cases. A young physician or other professional, with considerable psychotherapeutic experience, generally sensitive to his patient's affective state, reasonably alert to the interaction between himself and his patient, although often ineffectual in attempting to alter that interaction, now has reached a landmark in his training. He is about to place the patient on the couch.

Robert Michels M.D.

Robert Michels

Robert Michels, M.D.

Robert Michels  

WHEN WE SEE A PATIENT, it is often helpful to have some notion as to the fantasy with which he approaches us, which structures his expectations and, often, the results of our treatment. So too, I thought that it might be interesting for you to hear the fantasy with which I approach my talk on this panel.

My fantasy begins next week. I see someone in consultation who tells me that he saw a brochure describing this program on "What Cures?" and, since he was interested in cure, he thought that he would seek out the panelists for help. He had done just that and, in fact, I was the fourth consultant he had seen that week.

The first consultant suggested that he really needed to understand the developmental psychodynamics of his neurotic process, and added that an understanding of his dominant unconscious fantasy that stemmed from the second to sixth years of his life might not help unless it was also accompanied by an understanding of his earlier years as well. The former would help him to understand his neurotic patterns of adaptation, while the latter would clarify the issues that led him to cling to those neurotic patterns so tenaciously.

My patient thanked his first consultant and went on to a second who, after hearing his story, said "Your problem seems to have begun in the social environment of your early development, and you are now preoccupied with a defensive retreat into imagination and fantasy that is dominating your existence.
